title: Align Your Structures: Structure Pretraining for Molecular Dynamics
one_liner: Split molecular dynamics generation into two stages: learn static structure shapes first, then learn how they move in time.
lead: Generating the dance of atoms over time (molecular dynamics) is hard because there is very little real trajectory data. This paper solves it by training on two separate problems: first, learn what single molecular shapes look like from a huge dataset of static structures, then learn the timing and motion from the smaller trajectory dataset. Like learning to draw a face before learning to animate it.

problem.h2: Why directly learning molecular movies fails
paras: A molecular dynamics trajectory is a movie: 100 frames showing atoms moving, bending, and rearranging. Each frame is a 3D snapshot of atomic positions and the atoms bonded together. You want to teach a neural network (a mathematical pattern-finder) to generate these movies from scratch, frame by frame, the way it generates image sequences.

A beginner would train one big model on trajectory data: give it one frame, predict the next frame, repeat. But there is almost no trajectory data available—labs run a few thousand real simulations, while millions of static structures (single snapshots) exist. The model is starving for examples.

Worse: each frame is its own puzzle. The network must learn to draw chemically plausible structures AND remember that atoms move smoothly from frame to frame. These are two separate problems competing for the model's learning focus. The model fails at both.

callout.html: Instead of learning trajectories whole, first master static structures, then layer on temporal flow.

panels.title: 1. The naive way: one big model
panels.caption: A single model tries to learn structures and motion at once. Starving for data.

panels.title: 2. The problem surfaces
panels.viz_args: Frame A → Frame B (atoms wrongly bonded, bad angle, atoms teleport)
panels.caption: Generated frames are chemically broken: bonds vanish, angles twist, atoms jump.

panels.title: 3. Structure pretraining: learn static shapes
panels.caption: Train on millions of static structures. Learn what bonded atoms look like.

panels.title: 4. Add temporal layers on top
panels.caption: Freeze structure knowledge. Add new layers that only learn how structures flow in time.

panels.title: 5. The payoff: realistic trajectories
panels.caption: Frames stay bonded, angles bend smoothly, atoms move in plausible paths.

steps.text: Use a diffusion model (a denoiser that learns to gradually add and remove noise) on millions of static molecular structures. It learns what valid bond angles and atom spacing look like.
Lock the learned structure knowledge. Do not change these weights.
Stack new trainable layers on top. These layers read the current frame and the previous frame and learn to blend them smoothly.
At each layer, interpolate: 70 percent frozen structure knowledge, 30 percent new temporal knowledge. As layers go deeper, the blend shifts.
Tune the temporal layers using the small trajectory dataset. The structure part already knows chemistry; the temporal part learns motion.

paras: Instead of one model, the paper uses two models stacked together. The bottom model is a frozen structure denoiser (learned from static data). The top layers are new trainable temporal modules that learn to move structures smoothly. The paper changes how these two talk to each other: at each layer, a linear mixing dial blends the structure signal with the motion signal.
object.object: The mixing weights between frozen structure layers and new temporal layers

hidden.name: How much of each frame's structure gets kept versus replaced
paras: The paper measures something called temporal consistency. This is not a noise level or a loss value—it is the degree to which consecutive frames are genuinely linked by plausible motion, not just random structural variations. When a bond angle changes by 2 degrees from frame to frame, that is consistent; if it jumps 45 degrees, it is broken.

The temporal interpolator enforces this by asking: does the structure model predict frame B's atoms look right? And do the temporal layers predict frame B flows smoothly from frame A? If both say yes, the interpolation succeeded.

heat.caption: Darker means weaker temporal alignment (atoms jump, bonds break, energies spike). Brighter means smooth, realistic motion.

reads.html: The paper's temporal layers learn to predict: given the previous frame, how should atoms move to stay bonded and make sense chemically?

The equivariant temporal interpolator couples the pretrained conformer denoiser with additional temporal linking layers, ensuring each frame stays statistically consistent with the overall trajectory statistics.

mechanism.h2: Why splitting the work makes it work
paras: The structure model has learned from millions of examples what atoms bonded together should look like: certain angles are plausible, certain distances are physical. This knowledge is brittle if you try to teach it trajectory dynamics simultaneously—it gets drowned out by motion noise.

By freezing it, the paper says: this part of the model will never be allowed to break chemical rules. Every frame it generates will automatically satisfy bond constraints. Now the temporal layers only have to solve one problem: make frames flow into each other smoothly. The model can focus.

The linear interpolation (70 percent structure, 30 percent temporal) makes this work. Early layers get more structure guidance (they are close to the frozen layers); later layers get more temporal guidance (they are where motion decisions happen). This glues the two problems together without letting one cancel the other out.

math.words: temporal output equals alpha times structure output plus one-minus-alpha times temporal-attention output, where alpha decreases layer-by-layer
math.equation: y_layer = alpha * structure(x) + (1 - alpha) * temporal(x, x_prev)
symbols: output of this layer in the mixed model
blend weight: how much structure vs. temporal (decreases as layers go up)
output from the frozen pretrained denoiser
output from new attention layers that see current and prior frames
the current frame's atom coordinates and features
the prior frame's atom coordinates and features

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Layer 1 (bottom, close to structure): alpha = 0.7, so output = 0.7 * structure(x) + 0.3 * temporal(x, x_prev). Structure dominates.
Layer 3 (middle): alpha = 0.5, so output = 0.5 * structure(x) + 0.5 * temporal(x, x_prev). Equal weight.
Layer 6 (top, close to motion): alpha = 0.2, so output = 0.2 * structure(x) + 0.8 * temporal(x, x_prev). Temporal dominates.
Result: bottom layers enforce atoms stay bonded; top layers coordinate smooth transitions. Both constraints satisfied together.

math.note: The dial at each layer tunes how much the frozen structure knowledge should override the learned temporal flow, ensuring chemical realism and realistic motion.

charts.title: Naive end-to-end model
charts.note: Model tries both problems at once and fails at both.

charts.title: Structure pretraining + temporal interpolator
charts.note: Each stage masters its own task. Combined result is realistic.

items.html: If the pretrained model has not learned chemistry well (e.g., trained on too few examples or on unclean data), then no amount of temporal layers will fix bad structures. The first stage is the foundation.

items.b: Temporal layers cannot recover from structure errors.
items.html: Since the structure model is frozen, if it outputs a chemically impossible atom position, the temporal layers cannot correct it. Frozen parts are frozen.

The paper uses fixed alpha values (70, 50, 30 percent at different layers). If the dataset requires a different blend—say, more structure emphasis on certain frames—the method cannot adjust. A learnable alpha could adapt the blend per-frame, which might catch finer temporal variations, but would require more training and make the model larger and slower.

items.b: Done right: pretraining data is large and clean.
items.html: If the conformer dataset is genuinely representative of real molecular shapes, and the trajectory dataset is accurate simulations, the method produces realistic movies.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Write a simple script that loads the pretrained structure model and the trained temporal interpolator. Feed it the first frame of a real trajectory (a snapshot of atom positions and bonds). Have the model generate the next 10 frames. Compare each generated frame to the real trajectory on three metrics: (1) Do generated atoms stay bonded to their partners or do bonds break? (2) Do atom positions drift smoothly or jump erratically? (3) Do the energies calculated from atomic positions fall within the plausible range or spike to infinity?
demo.metric_eq: temporal_smoothness = average of (distance_moved from frame t to t+1) for all atoms. Lower variance = smoother. bond_preservation = fraction of bonds that stay within plausible distance in all frames. energy_validity = fraction of frames with energies in the range of real simulations.
demo.closing: A good demo makes it impossible to ignore that the generated trajectory moves like real atoms: smooth, chemically coherent, never teleporting or breaking bonds, because the pretrained structure model enforces chemical realism and the temporal layers enforce smooth transitions.
